planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in cool, moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade, in a sheltered site protected from wind and afternoon sun; like its Japanese relative, Diphylleia sinensis resents root disturbance and establishes slowly.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall into cool, consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade, choosing a sheltered north-facing site protected from wind and hot afternoon sun. Diphylleia sinensis is a Chinese woodland relative of the better-known Japanese skeleton flower, forming a clump of large, deeply lobed, umbrella-like peltate leaves topped in late spring by small, flat-topped clusters of white flowers; unlike D. grayi, its petals stay opaque even when soaked by rain rather than turning transparent. Clusters of glossy, deep blue berries follow on reddish stalks in summer, giving a second season of ornament similar to its American and Japanese relatives. It demands constant cool moisture and a humus-rich woodland soil, and is slow to settle in after transplanting, so choose a permanent site and avoid moving established clumps.

planting.note: Divide rhizomatous clumps in spring, or plant container-grown starts, into moist to moderately dry, humus-rich soil in full to part shade; the white leaf stripes hold their color best out of hot direct sun, which can scorch the pale variegated tissue.

directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist to moderately dry, humus-rich soil in full to part shade, keeping the pale variegated foliage out of hot afternoon sun, which can scorch the lighter tissue. 'Variegata' carries the same low, arching, strap-like rosettes and slow, rhizome-spreading habit as the species, but each leaf is striped lengthwise in creamy white to pale yellow, giving a brighter, more refined look to the deep-shade groundcover role that plain green jade lily fills. Small, fragrant, pale pink flowers open low among the foliage in autumn, followed by red berries, though the variegated leaves remain the main ornamental feature through the year. Grow it as a collector's accent along a shaded path edge or in a container, since it spreads more slowly than the species and stays useful at a smaller scale for years before needing division.

subcategory: hardy Himalayan ginger relative with orchid-like flowers

planting.note: Plant fleshy root divisions 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Roscoea humeana emerges later than most spring perennials, so mark the site and avoid disturbing what looks like bare soil.

directions: Plant fleshy root divisions 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, marking the site since growth does not appear until quite late in spring. Roscoea humeana is a compact, cold-hardy Chinese species from the mountains of Yunnan and Sichuan, forming a low rosette of broad, upright leaves and producing large, richly colored orchid-like flowers in shades of purple, violet, or occasionally white or yellow, generally opening earlier in the season and closer to the ground than the taller R. cautleyoides or R. purpurea. Sharp winter drainage is essential, since the fleshy storage roots rot quickly in cold, waterlogged soil, and a dry winter mulch is helpful in heavier clay gardens. Combine with hostas, hardy ferns, and hellebores in a woodland or shaded rock garden setting in zones 5-9.

subcategory: hardy Himalayan ginger relative with orchid-like flowers

planting.note: Plant fleshy root divisions 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; like other roscoea, this Yunnan native emerges late in spring and should not be disturbed while apparently dormant.

directions: Plant fleshy root divisions 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; like other roscoea, this Yunnan native emerges late in spring and should not be disturbed while the site still looks bare. Roscoea scillifolia is distinguished from other cultivated roscoea species by its unusually narrow, grass-like or squill-like foliage, quite different from the broader strap-shaped leaves typical of the genus, above which it bears the same two-lipped, orchid-like flowers in shades of purple to violet-pink in mid to late summer. It tends to flower a little earlier in the season than R. cautleyoides in many gardens and stays more compact, making it a good choice for the front of a shaded border or a trough planting. Provide sharp winter drainage to prevent rot of the fleshy roots, and mulch lightly for winter protection in colder parts of its range.

subcategory: hardy Himalayan ginger relative with orchid-like flowers

planting.note: Plant fleshy root divisions 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; 'Kew Beauty' emerges late like other roscoea selections, so mark the planting site to avoid disturbing dormant roots.

directions: Plant fleshy root divisions 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, and be patient with its late spring emergence. 'Kew Beauty' is a long-grown, highly regarded selection of the variable species Roscoea cautleyoides, chosen for its especially large, clear pale-yellow to cream flowers held well above the narrow, upright foliage in early to midsummer, a softer and more luminous color than the straight species typically offers. It shares the same essential requirement for sharp winter drainage as other roscoea, since the fleshy storage roots are prone to rot in cold, wet soil, and benefits from a gritty soil amendment in heavier gardens. A choice, long-lived addition to a shaded woodland or rock garden border, pairing well with hostas and hardy ferns.

subcategory: hardy Himalayan ginger relative with orchid-like purple flowers

planting.note: Plant fleshy root divisions 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; 'Red Gurkha' emerges late like the species, so mark the site to avoid disturbing dormant roots.

directions: Plant fleshy root divisions 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, marking the site since growth does not appear until late spring. 'Red Gurkha' is a well-known wild-collected selection of Roscoea purpurea originally gathered in Nepal, prized for flowers in a much deeper wine-red to maroon-purple than the violet-purple typical of the species, giving an unusually rich, saturated color to the two-lipped, orchid-like blooms of early to midsummer. In all other respects it grows and behaves like the species, forming a compact rosette of upright, strap-shaped leaves and demanding the same sharp winter drainage to prevent rot of its fleshy storage roots. An excellent choice for gardeners wanting more color range than the standard lavender-purple roscoea offers in a shaded or woodland border, zones 6-9.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil at the margin of a stream, pond, or bog in partial shade in spring; 'Miller's Crimson' comes reasonably true from isolated seed, but named-clump division guarantees the deep color.

directions: Plant divisions or container-grown plants into consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade beside a stream, pond, or bog garden, allowing it to self-sow where conditions stay reliably damp. 'Miller's Crimson' is one of the oldest and most widely grown named selections of Japanese candelabra primrose, chosen for flowers in a rich, deep crimson-red rather than the more common magenta-pink of seed-grown plants, held in the same stacked whorls on tall stems from late spring into early summer. Because open-pollinated seedlings can drift back toward the species' typical pink tones over time, isolate the planting from other primrose colors or propagate named clumps by division to keep the deep crimson color true. Pair with hostas, astilbes, and ferns in a permanently moist, partially shaded water-garden setting, and expect the foliage to die back completely in hot, dry summer weather.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil at the margin of a stream, pond, or bog in partial shade in spring; isolate from colored primrose forms if self-sown seedlings are wanted to stay true white.

directions: Plant divisions or container-grown plants into consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade beside a stream, pond, or bog garden. 'Postford White' is a classic named selection of Japanese candelabra primrose bred for pure white flowers with a small yellow eye, a clean and luminous contrast to the crimson, magenta, and pink tones of typical seed-grown Japanese primrose, held in the same tiered, candelabra-like whorls on tall stems in late spring and early summer. It combines especially well with pink- or crimson-flowered primrose selections such as 'Miller's Crimson' to build a layered color display along a shaded streambank or pond margin. Isolate plantings from other primrose colors if seed-grown offspring are wanted to stay true white, since open pollination with colored forms produces mixed results, and keep the soil constantly moist through the growing season to prevent premature summer dormancy.

common_name: Dawn Ansell Japanese Star Primrose (Hose-in-Hose White)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring before new growth or in early fall; like the species, 'Dawn Ansell' is winter-dormant and disappears completely below ground from midsummer through late winter, so mark the planting site.

directions: Plant divisions in early spring, just before new growth appears, into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, marking the site since the plant vanishes completely below ground each summer. 'Dawn Ansell' is a widely admired British-raised selection of Japanese star primrose noted for its unusual hose-in-hose flowers -- each pale, greenish-white bloom appears to have a second smaller flower nested inside it -- a distinctive form among the huge range of sieboldii cultivars developed over centuries in Japan. The finely textured, crinkled leaves emerge alongside the flowers in early spring and persist only until early summer before the plant goes fully dormant, an adaptation well suited to dry woodland shade later in the season. Divide congested clumps carefully while dormant or just as new growth appears, since this cultivar is propagated only by division and does not come true from seed.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall or very early spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to dappled sun; 'Katy McSparron' is a sport that must be propagated by division to keep its variegation, since seedlings revert to plain green.

directions: Plant divisions in fall or very early spring into moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to dappled sun; 'Katy McSparron' is a sport of the common cowslip selected for its rounded, softly puckered leaves broadly splashed and streaked with creamy gold-yellow, providing garden interest well before the fragrant, nodding yellow flowers open in mid-spring on short stems. Because the variegation is a genetically unstable sport, it must be propagated by division of an established clump rather than by seed, since seedlings revert to plain green foliage. The bright leaves hold their color best with a little morning sun or dappled shade rather than deep, dry shade, where variegation tends to fade. Divide congested clumps every few years in fall to maintain vigor and share the true variegated form.
